lead: An aircraft rarely knows its position directly. It measures something small — the time a radio pulse takes to return, the angle a beam arrives from, the difference in distance to two stations — and turns that number into a line on a map. Every point on that line would have given the same reading. Cross two such lines and you have a fix. This chapter builds the geometry behind that: the surface, the words for direction, the shapes of the lines, and how the crossing angle sets the size of the error.
prereq: You need basic trigonometry and the air data instruments of Unit 3 (airspeed indicator and altimeter) for the third dimension.

blocks.text: Navigation starts with a model of the Earth. The simplest is a sphere. A meridian is a great circle through both poles; the equator is the great circle at right angles to it. Latitude φ is the angle from the equator, 0° to 90° north or south. Longitude λ is the angle east or west of Greenwich, 0° to 180°.

The real Earth is flattened at the poles, so a sphere would misplace a point by up to about 21 km. The standard shape is an ellipsoid of revolution called WGS-84, with semi-major axis a = 6 378 137 m and flattening f = 1/298.257223563. Satellite orbits and GPS coordinates are expressed on this ellipsoid, so it is not an academic detail.

A great circle is the shortest surface path between two points; its plane passes through the Earth's centre. A rhumb line keeps a constant track and cuts every meridian at the same angle. It is easier to fly but longer, except along a meridian or the equator.
The nautical mile is 1852 m, originally one minute of arc of latitude. One knot is one nautical mile per hour. Navigation distances are in nautical miles and speeds in knots.
d = R · Δσ,   cos Δσ = sin φ₁ sin φ₂ + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ
blocks.where: d is the great-circle distance in metres; R ≈ 6 371 000 m is a mean Earth radius; φ₁ and φ₂ are the two latitudes; Δλ is the difference in longitude; Δσ is the angular separation in radians.

blocks.text: Heading is where the nose points, measured clockwise from north. It is an aircraft quantity, and you must say true or magnetic.
Track is where the aircraft actually moves over the ground. It is a ground quantity. Wind separates track from heading.
Bearing is the direction of one point from another. Name both points: the bearing of the station from the aircraft differs from the bearing of the aircraft from the station by 180°.

Radial is a line leaving a station outward, named by its magnetic bearing from that station. An aircraft on the 030 radial sits somewhere on the line that leaves the station at 030°. Its heading can be anything.
Drift is the angle between heading and track caused by wind, positive to the right. Track = heading + drift. Ground speed is measured along the track; true airspeed along the heading.
A line of position (LOP) is the set of all points on the Earth where one measurement would give the same reading. Three shapes matter.

items: Circle: a range from a known station fixes distance but not direction, so the LOP is a circle centred on the station. DME, GNSS and radar give circles.
Straight line: a bearing from a known station fixes direction but not distance, so the LOP is a line leaving the station. VOR, ADF and the ILS localizer give lines.
Hyperbola: the difference in range to two stations is constant along a curve with the stations as foci. That curve is a hyperbola.

blocks.text: Fix methods take their names from the measurements: rho-theta (one range and one bearing from the same station), rho-rho (two ranges, two circles) and theta-theta (two bearings, two lines).
Two LOPs cross at a point — the fix. Three lines almost never meet at one point; they form a small triangle called the cocked hat, and the fix is assumed inside it.
The cut angle θ is the angle at which the two LOPs cross. Position uncertainty is largest along each line, so the fix is tightest when the cut is near 90° and poor when the lines run nearly parallel.

blocks.where: σ is the 1-sigma position error along each line of position; θ is the cut angle. At θ = 90° the fix error equals σ; at θ = 30° it doubles.

sections.h3: Reference frames, and two kinds of good

blocks.text: ECEF (Earth-centred, Earth-fixed): origin at the Earth's centre, x-axis through the equator at Greenwich, z-axis through the north pole, y-axis completing a right-handed set. The frame turns with the Earth, so a ground point has fixed coordinates. Satellite systems broadcast in ECEF.
Local NED: origin at the aircraft, axes north, east, down. This is the frame the pilot and the flight management system use; heading and track live here.
Inertial: fixed in space, not turning with the Earth. Gyros and accelerometers sense motion here. Earth rate is 15.041° per hour — small, but not zero over a long flight.

Accuracy is how close the reported position is to the true one. Repeatability is how close repeated measurements are to each other. A system can be repeatable and wrong: a fixed bias shifts every fix by the same 200 m. Calibration removes bias; averaging removes noise; neither removes the other.

figure.caption: Each measurement gives one line of position; two lines crossing at a wide angle give a small error ellipse, which is the fix.

spec.title: From one measurement to a fix
spec.aria: A flow from a reference frame through one measurement to a single line of position, then two or more lines crossing to give a fix with its error ellipse.

examples.question: Two DME stations A and B are 130 nm apart on the ground. The aircraft's corrected DME reads 50 nm to A and 120 nm to B. (a) Find the cut angle at which the two range circles cross. (b) Find the aircraft's distance from A measured along the line AB, and its perpendicular distance from AB. (c) Judge the quality of the fix.
steps: The three sides of the triangle A–aircraft–B are 50 nm, 120 nm and 130 nm.
Check with Pythagoras: 50² + 120² = 2500 + 14400 = 16900 = 130². The triangle is right-angled at the aircraft, which confirms θ = 90°.
A 90° cut gives sin θ = 1, so the fix error equals the error along a single line — the best a two-range fix can achieve.
examples.answer: The circles cross at θ = 90°; the aircraft lies 19.23 nm from A along AB and 46.15 nm off that line, which is a well-conditioned two-range fix.
examples.check:
import math
dA, dB, dAB = 50.0, 120.0, 130.0
cosT = (dA**2 + dB**2 - dAB**2) / (2 * dA * dB)
theta = math.degrees(math.acos(cosT))
x = (dA**2 - dB**2 + dAB**2) / (2 * dAB)
h = math.sqrt(dA**2 - x**2)
print(round(theta, 2))
print(round(x, 2))
print(round(h, 2))

traps: Bearing, heading and track are three different things. A radial of 030° says where the aircraft sits relative to the station; the nose may point anywhere.
Outbound on the 030 radial you track 030°; inbound on the same radial you track 210°. Forgetting the 180° flip costs marks.
A rhumb line is not a great circle. Constant heading is not the shortest path, and the gap widens with latitude.
A small cocked hat does not prove a good fix. If all three lines share one systematic bias — a common timing error, say — they make a tiny triangle around a wrong point.
1 nm = 1852 m and 1 kt = 1 nm/h. Mixing knots with km/h gives a factor 1.852 error in every wind-triangle answer.

quiz.a: The set of all points on the Earth's surface at which one particular measurement would give the same reading.

quiz.q: Give the nautical mile in metres and define the knot.
quiz.a: 1 nm = 1852 m; 1 knot = 1 nautical mile per hour.

quiz.q: Why is a rhumb line longer than the great circle between the same two points?
quiz.a: A rhumb line keeps a constant angle to every meridian, so it spirals toward the pole instead of taking the shortest surface path; the two coincide only on a meridian or the equator.

quiz.q: An aircraft is on the 090 radial of a VOR. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you?
quiz.a: It tells you the aircraft lies on the line leaving the station at 090° (to the east of it). It does not give distance from the station, nor heading, nor track.

quiz.q: Two DME ranges read 50 nm and 70 nm from stations 100 nm apart. Find the cut angle and the fix error if each line has a 1-sigma error of 1 nm.
An aircraft has heading 070° (T) and drift 8° to the right. Find the track.
Two LOPs cross at 30° with a 1-sigma error of 1 nm each. Compare this fix with a 90° cut.
quiz.a: Fix error = σ ÷ sin θ = 1 ÷ sin 30° = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 nm, twice the 1 nm obtained at a 90° cut. A shallow cut stretches the error ellipse along the bisector of the lines.

quiz.q: A fix has a very small cocked hat. Why can it still be badly wrong?
quiz.a: Random errors make the hat large; correlated systematic errors — a common clock bias or a wrongly surveyed station — shift all three lines together and leave a small triangle around a biased point. Size alone does not prove accuracy.

beyond: Not for the exam. The σ ÷ sin θ argument reappears in satellite navigation as dilution of precision, generalised to four satellites and written as a matrix. Civil aviation adds receiver autonomous integrity monitoring, which checks whether the satellite geometry still supports the required accuracy, and required navigation performance approach design, which is pure cut-angle thinking. Inertial and satellite data are blended in the frames described above. Useful search terms: WGS-84 parameters, dilution of precision, great-circle sailing, required navigation performance.
